Julia laughed, a little watery sound in the darkness. "A contract! Oh, Jim, you make everything sound so practical, so surgical!"

"It's the most practical thing in the world," he insisted. "You and me. Everything else is just details. Think of all the things we have to do first. We have to get you to New York. I have to show you the spot in Central Park where I fell off a donkey when I was seven. You have to see a real blizzard. I have to see you see a real blizzard."

"And what do I have to do?" she asked softly, her cheek resting against the rough wool of his jacket.

"You," he said, and she could hear the smile in his voice, "you just have to be there. You have to let me buy you silly hats, and you have to get used to me rumpling your hair, and you have to promise you'll never stop looking at me as if I've just given you the moon."

"But you have," she whispered. "You have."

"I was terrified of you, you know," he confessed suddenly, his tone changing. "That first night, at the Farquhars' dinner. You were so quiet. So still. You had on a dark blue dress, and you were watching everybody. I thought you were judging us all."

"I was!" Julia said, with a little gasp of laughter. "I was judging everything! I felt as if I'd been dropped on a strange planet, and I was trying to learn the language. I thought you were the king of the planet, so handsome and sure of yourself. I was mostly terrified you would speak to me."

"And I was terrified you wouldn't," he finished for her. "Funny, isn't it?"

Before she could answer, there was a cheerful halloo from down the lane, and the crunch of footsteps on the gravel.

"There you are! Hiding in the dark!" It was Barbara's voice, clear as a bell. "Honestly, Julia, you'll catch your death of cold, and then what will Jim do for a bride on Tuesday? For shame, Doctor, letting your patient get chilled!"

Jim stood up, pulling Julia with him, tucking her hand firmly into the crook of his arm. "She's not my patient, she's my girl," he said, with a happy sort of defiance. "And I'm keeping her warm."

The walk back to the house was a merry affair. The other young people, Tom Toland and a cousin visiting from the East, kept up a stream of lighthearted teasing. Julia found herself included, not as an outsider, but as one half of a happy conspiracy. They treated her with a gentle, affectionate reverence, as if her great good fortune in capturing Jim Studdiford had made her something special and rare. It was a new feeling, and a heady one.

At the wide, welcoming porch of the Toland house, the group finally paused. The night air was growing cooler, and the lights from inside spilled out in golden rectangles onto the lawn.

"Well, I suppose it's time to turn in," said Mrs. Toland, appearing in the doorway, a soft shawl around her shoulders. "Julia, my dear, you look tired. You've had a long day."

"A wonderful day, Mrs. Toland," Julia said, her voice full of a sincerity that made the older woman smile.

The young men said their goodnights, and soon it was only Jim and Julia left on the porch, under the dim yellow light. The others had tactfully disappeared inside.

"I'll have to go," he said reluctantly. "I'm staying on the launch. Dad's orders. Said it would look better."

"Look better?"

"Not to be under the same roof until we're married," he explained, a wry grin on his face. "Even a roof as big as the Tolands'. My father is a great man for the proprieties."

"He sounds a little bit frightening," Julia admitted.

"Nah," Jim said, dismissing it with a wave of his hand. "He's all bark. You'll have him eating out of your hand in five minutes. Just like you have me." He cupped her face in his hands, his thumbs stroking her cheeks. "Sleep well, Ju. Dream of New York."

"I'll dream of you," she corrected him.

"Same thing," he said, and kissed her, a quick, warm kiss full of promise. And then he was gone, his footsteps echoing down the path toward the water.

Julia went inside, her heart singing. Barbara was waiting for her at the top of the stairs.

"Well?" she said, hands on her hips. "Did he behave himself?"

"Barbara, you're awful!" Julia laughed.

"Somebody has to be," Barbara said matter of factly. "Come on. I saved you some of the cold chicken. You ate nothing at dinner, you were too busy making eyes at your young man."

The next day was Sunday, a day of glorious, lazy sunshine. After a late breakfast on the veranda, surrounded by newspapers and the scent of climbing roses, Julia felt a sudden pang of duty.

"Barbara," she said, setting down her coffee cup with resolve. "I simply must write some of my notes. All those packages--I can't bear to think of them sitting there unanswered."

"Oh, fiddle," Barbara said. "You have the rest of your life to write thank you notes. But if you must, you must. There's paper in the desk in the library. Just remember what I told you. Short and smart."

Julia found herself alone in the big, cool library, with its walls of books and the scent of leather and lemon polish. On the massive mahogany desk lay a stack of creamy notepaper, monogrammed with Barbara's initials. Julia picked up a pen and a list of gifts and givers. 'Jam pot from the Fowlers,' the first item read.

She dipped the pen in the inkwell. 'Dear Mrs. Fowler,' she began. 'It was so very kind of you to think of us. The jam pot is perfectly lovely, and we shall think of you whenever we use it.' She stopped, chewing the end of her pen. It sounded stiff. It didn't sound like her at all. It didn't begin to express the wave of astonished gratitude she felt that these people, these strangers, would send her, Julia Page, a beautiful object for her new life.

She tried again. 'Dear Mrs. Fowler, I could have cried when I saw the beautiful jam pot! To think that you would be so kind--' No, that was all wrong. That was the old Julia, the girl who was surprised by any kindness at all. Barbara would call her a 'poor webfoot' for writing such a thing.

She sighed, and stared out the window at the shimmering bay. This new life, it seemed, had its own rules, its own language. It was not just a matter of new frocks and going to the theatre; it was a whole new way of feeling, or at least, of expressing what one felt. 'The shorter they are the smarter they are,' Barbara had said. Smartness seemed a very cold and distant virtue.

Just then, she heard his voice in the hall, and the sound of it was like a key turning in a lock, opening up all the joy inside her.

"Where is she? Where's my girl?"

A moment later, Jim was in the doorway, his hair bright in the sunlight, his face alight with a smile that was just for her.

"Hiding in here with all these dusty old books?" he teased, coming over to the desk. "Barbara said I'd find you slaving away." He looked down at the half written notes. "Good heavens, Julie, don't tell me you're doing homework on a Sunday."

"I have to," she said, feeling suddenly shy. "I don't want people to think I'm ungrateful."

"Ungrateful? You?" He laughed, a big, hearty sound that filled the quiet room. "You're the most grateful soul I ever met. You're grateful for a sunny day, or a good cup of coffee. "But where are we going?" she asked, as he pulled her to her feet.

"It's a surprise," he said. "Put on a hat. A practical one. We're going exploring."

She closed her eyes, and he led her by the hand a few paces over uneven ground. She could hear the wind in the trees and the distant cry of a gull.

"Okay," he said, his voice close to her ear. "Open them."

She opened her eyes. They were standing on a wide, cleared patch of land at the very top of the hill. Below them, the world fell away in a breathtaking sweep. The bay was a sheet of dazzling blue, dotted with white sails. Alcatraz was a dark smudge, and beyond it, across the water, San Francisco lay like a toy city, hazy and beautiful in the afternoon light. But it was not the view that made her gasp.

It was the house.

Or rather, the beginnings of a house. A foundation had been laid, and the timber frame of the first floor rose up into the clean, bright air, a skeleton of fresh-cut wood that smelled wonderfully of pine and sawdust.

"Jim," she breathed. "What is this?"

"This," he said, his arm circling her waist, his voice full of a quiet, proud joy, "is home. Or it's going to be."

She could not speak. She simply stared. It was big, much bigger than she had imagined. It faced the view, with wide spaces for windows that would drink in the light and the sea and the sky.

"Is it--is it ours?" she whispered, the question sounding foolish even to her own ears.

"Of course it's ours, you goose!" he said, hugging her tight. "I bought the land last year. I thought, someday, the girl I marry will want to live here. And then I met you, and I told the builders to get a move on."

He led her through the skeletal rooms, his voice eager and excited as he pointed everything out. "This will be the living room. Big fireplace here, for foggy nights. And this, this is the dining room, with french doors that will open out onto a terrace. Can't you just see it, Julie? We'll have breakfast out here in the summer."

He led her to another space, a large, airy room that looked directly out at the Golden Gate. "And this is for you. Your studio, or a sitting room, whatever you want it to be. A place where you can be quiet and read your poetry books and not be bothered."

Julia touched the raw wood of a window frame, her fingers tracing the grain. It felt solid, real. It was one thing to hear him talk of their future, of houses and sailing and quiet mornings. It was another thing entirely to stand inside it, to feel its shape around her. A wave of emotion so powerful it almost buckled her knees washed over her. It was joy, but it was also a kind of fear. This solid, beautiful, expensive house was for her, Julia Page, the girl who had grown up in a boarding house, who had mended her own stockings and counted her pennies for a new book.

"It's too much," she said, her voice trembling. "Jim, it's too beautiful. I don't deserve it."

He turned her to face him, his hands gentle on her shoulders, his expression suddenly serious. The teasing light was gone from his eyes, replaced by a deep, searching tenderness.

"Don't ever say that," he said, his voice low. "Don't ever, ever say that, Julie. You think I'm the lucky one, the one who was born with everything. And maybe I was. But none of it, not the money, not the work, not any of it meant a thing until I found you. You're not getting what you deserve, darling. I am. I'm the one who's getting a thousand times more than he deserves."

He saw the tears shimmering in her eyes, and his face softened. "Ah, Ju, don't cry. Please don't cry. Or if you have to, cry for happiness."

"I am," she sobbed, laughing through her tears. "I am, you idiot!"

He pulled a clean handkerchief from his pocket. "Here," he said, dabbing at her eyes as gently as if she were a child. "We can't have you spoiling this face. Now. I want to show you where the kitchen will be. It's going to have the very latest thing in gas stoves. And a pantry big enough to get lost in. You'll like that, won't you?"

She took the handkerchief and blew her nose. "Yes," she said, her voice still thick with tears. "I'll like that very much."

They spent another hour there, walking through the imaginary rooms, planning where the furniture would go, where they would plant roses, where their children, spoken of in hushed and reverent tones, would one day play. Jim was full of practical plans, and Julia was full of a dazed, wondering joy. This wasn't a dream. This was their life, being built board by board, right in front of her. The girl who had learned things so hard was finally learning the simple, astonishing lesson of happiness.

As they drove back down the hill, with the setting sun turning the sky to orange and rose, Julia leaned her head against Jim's shoulder. The wind whipped her hair, and the engine rattled companionably.

"Jim," she said.

"Yes, darling?"

"Thank you."

He glanced down at her, a quick, warm look. "For what? For a pile of lumber?"

"For everything," she said. "For showing me."

He didn't ask what she meant. He seemed to understand. He just reached over and took her hand, his strong fingers lacing through hers, and held it all the way back to the Tolands' waiting house. That night, when Julia sat down again at the big mahogany desk, she pushed aside the half finished, stilted notes. She took a fresh sheet of paper, dipped the pen in the ink, and wrote in her own, clear hand.

'Dear Mrs. Fowler,' she wrote. 'Thank you for the jam pot. It is the first thing I have received for my new home with Jim, and I shall treasure it always.'

It was short. And Barbara, she thought with a little smile, would probably even think it was smart. But it was also, entirely, the truth.

"They won't be thinking about your handwriting. They'll glance at the signature, say 'Oh, how nice, she wrote,' and then they'll use the silver bowl to put olives in. That's how it works. Jim's mother will be the one who really pays attention, anyway." "His mother?" Julia asked, a little nervously. She had not yet met Mrs. Studdiford, who had been traveling in Europe and was only arriving that evening. "Oh, yes. She's a stickler for the proprieties. But she's a dear, really. She'll adore you. Just look helpless and pretty, and she'll want to take you under her wing immediately." Barbara grinned. "It's her favorite occupation. Now, stop worrying. Write 'Thank you so much for the beautiful silver bowl. Jim and I are so looking forward to using it.' Sign your name with a flourish, and you're done. See? Simple." Julia took a sip of the cool tea and picked up her pen again. Simple for Barbara, perhaps. For her, it was another lesson in a new and bewildering language. But as she wrote, a strange thing happened. With each note she finished, the names became a little less intimidating, the task a little less daunting. She was Julia Page Studdiford. They would know who she was fast enough. The wedding day dawned clear and bright, one of those perfect California days that felt polished by the sea. Julia awoke to a sense of ceremonial chaos. Aunt Sanna was directing traffic in and out of her room, Barbara was issuing commands, and below her window, she could hear the crunch of gravel as cars began to arrive. She was bathed and perfumed and dressed as if she were a doll, her trembling hands fumbling with the tiny seed pearls on her satin gown. It was a simple dress, but to Julia it was the most beautiful thing she had ever owned, shimmering with a light that seemed to come from within. When she was finally ready, Barbara shooed everyone out of the room. "There," she said, turning Julia to face the long mirror. "Take a look." Julia stared. The girl in the mirror was a stranger, her face pale and her eyes enormous and dark. Her hair was swept up under a cloud of white tulle, and the simple white dress made her look taller, more serene. It was not the girl from the cannery, not the girl who had felt eighty years old beside Jim's youth. This was someone new. This was Mrs. James Studdiford. A knock came at the door. "Five minutes, Julie," said a man's voice--Mr. Toland's. "Jim's down there looking like he's about to perform his first surgery all over again." Julia laughed, a shaky little sound. "I'm ready," she said, her voice a whisper. Walking down the wide, flower-decked staircase on Mr. Toland's arm was a slow, deliberate dream. She saw a sea of faces, all turned toward her, all smiling. She saw sunlight streaming through the windows, glinting on silver and crystal. And then she saw Jim, standing at the foot of the stairs, his face serious and impossibly dear, his eyes locked on hers. All her nervousness vanished, replaced by a wave of love so powerful it was like a physical force, pulling her toward him. The ceremony was a blur. The scent of lilies, the low murmur of the minister's voice, the solid warmth of Jim's hand holding hers. She heard him say, "I will," his voice so strong and certain it seemed to vibrate in the very air around them. And she heard her own voice, surprisingly steady, make the same promise. Then he was lifting her veil, and his face was close, his eyes full of a light she had never seen before. "Hello, wife," he murmured, just before he kissed her, and the room erupted in a happy storm of laughter and applause. The reception was a joyful whirlwind. People kissed her cheek and shook her hand, calling her "Mrs. Studdiford," and with each repetition the name sounded a little more like her own. She saw Barbara deep in conversation with a handsome young man, and Janey Toland shyly guarding the gift table, on which Julia spied not one, but three enormous sets of carvers. She ate cake, and drank a sip of champagne that made her nose tingle, and laughed until her cheeks ached. And through it all, Jim was there, his hand at her elbow, his arm around her waist, his presence a constant, reassuring anchor in the happy chaos. Then, all too soon, it was time to go. Barbara whisked her upstairs to change into a smart blue traveling suit. "Now, for heaven's sake, don't cry," Barbara commanded, fussing with Julia's hat. "Your honeymoon is not the time for a red nose." "I'm not crying," Julia said, though her throat felt tight. "I'm just--I'm too happy." "Good," said Barbara, giving her a quick, firm hug. "You deserve it. Now go on, your husband is waiting." They ran down the stairs together, through a shower of rice and good-natured shouts, to the big motorcar that was waiting for them, an old shoe tied ridiculously to the back. Jim bundled her in and jumped in beside her, and with a roar and a final wave, they were off, leaving the cheering crowd behind. As the car sped them toward the ferry building, Julia leaned her head back against the leather seat and let out a long sigh. Jim took her gloved hand. "Tired?" "Exhausted," she admitted. "And I think I have rice in my hair." "A small price to pay," he said, smiling. He lifted her hand and kissed her fingers. "Well, Mrs. Studdiford? We did it." "We did it," she echoed softly. She looked at him, at her husband, and a feeling of profound, quiet peace settled over her. The flurry was over. The rest of their life was beginning. The journey east was an adventure in itself. Julia had never been on a train for more than a few hours, and the idea of sleeping and eating while the world slid past her window was a constant source of wonder. They had a private compartment, a cozy world of polished wood and green plush seats. For three days, they watched the green hills of California flatten into the vast, empty plains of the heartland, and then resolve again into the rolling, wooded country of the east. They talked for hours, learning the small, secret histories of each other's lives. Julia told him about her grandmother, about the little economies and the quiet despairs of her childhood, and he listened with a tender gravity that made her feel, for the first time, that her past was not something to be hidden, but simply a part of the person he loved. He told her about his own lonely boyhood in a big, quiet house, with a famous father who was always busy, and a delicate mother who was always resting. "That's why I seem so young, I think," he explained one afternoon, as they sat watching the telegraph poles tick by. "I had to be so grown-up as a boy, so quiet and responsible. When I finally got to college, I suppose I just went a little wild with the sheer fun of it all. I'm making up for lost time." "And I'm trying to catch up to all the time I lost being old," she said thoughtfully. "We'll meet in the middle," he promised, and kissed her. They ate in the dining car, a marvel of crisp white linen and gleaming silver, served by waiters who balanced trays with impossible grace as the train swayed and clattered along the tracks. At night, their little compartment was transformed into a snug bedroom, and Julia would lie in her berth, listening to the rhythmic song of the wheels on the rails, the lonesome whistle in the dark, with Jim sleeping just across from her. It was an intimacy so new, so profound, it filled her with a quiet awe. On the fourth morning, he woke her early. "Come and look, sleepyhead." She went to the window, and gasped. Outside, the world was a canyon of stone and glass, buildings so tall they seemed to scrape the pale morning sky. The air was thick with a hazy smoke, and the streets below, even at this early hour, were teeming with a frantic energy unlike anything she had ever seen. "This isn't a city," she whispered. "It's a whole world." "This," said Jim, his arm around her shoulders, "is New York." The grandeur of the station, the sheer press of humanity, the cacophony of automobile horns and vendors' cries on the street--it all washed over Julia in a dizzying wave. A taxi took them to their hotel on Fifth Avenue, a palace of marble and gold leaf, where a doorman in livery swept the door open for them and a silent elevator whisked them up to their suite. The rooms were beautiful, decorated in pale silks and furnished with graceful, delicate chairs. A vase of yellow roses stood on a table, and through the wide windows, Julia could see a corner of a vast green park. She walked to the window and stood there, looking out, her hands clasped before her. She felt Jim come up behind her, his hands resting on her shoulders. "What are you thinking about?" he asked gently. She was thinking of a line from a book she had once read, about a view of all the kingdoms of the world. She felt like that, as if she were standing on a great height, surveying a new and promised land. It was her kingdom now, this world of beauty and ease and love. Her home. "And some, like myself," she whispered, echoing the words she had said to him what felt like a lifetime ago, "are born in the bad belt, and push into the good! And we're the really lucky ones!" He turned her and kissed her, a long, slow kiss full of promise and homecoming. "You angel," he murmured against her lips. Later, after they had bathed and changed, and dined in their rooms on delicate food served under silver covers, Jim grew restless. "It's a crime to be in New York and sit in a hotel room," he declared, pacing the floor. "Even a very nice hotel room. Let's go out! Let's see a show." "A show?" Julia said, startled. "But Jim, it must be nearly nine o'clock! And I'm not--I don't have the right sort of dress." "Nonsense," he said. "You look beautiful. And this is New York! The shows are just starting. We'll go to the Ziegfeld Follies. I'll have the concierge get us tickets." And so, in a whirlwind of activity that left Julia breathless, she found herself putting on her best silk frock, the one she had thought far too grand for anything but the most formal occasion, while Jim telephoned downstairs. An hour later they were in a taxi, speeding through the glittering streets toward a blaze of light that spelled out "Broadway." The theatre was a fantasy of red velvet, gold leaf, and shimmering crystal chandeliers. It was filled with the most beautiful people Julia had ever seen. The women were draped in silks and satins, sparkling with jewels; the men were impossibly elegant in black evening clothes. Julia felt a fresh wave of panic, a certainty that she was a fraud, a little brown wren who had accidentally flown into a cage of brilliant, exotic birds. "Chin up, Mrs. Studdiford," Jim whispered in her ear as an usher led them to their seats in the front of the orchestra. "You're the prettiest girl here, and I should know. I've looked." And then the lights went down, the orchestra swelled, and the curtain rose on a scene of such spectacular, glittering excess that Julia gasped. There were dozens of girls, all impossibly long-legged and beautiful, wearing fantastic costumes of feathers and rhinestones. There were comedians who made the whole audience roar with laughter, and singers whose voices filled the vast theatre. It was loud, it was gaudy, it was utterly magnificent. Julia sat forward in her seat, her eyes shining, completely captivated. All her fears, all her insecurities, melted away in the sheer, dazzling joy of the spectacle. She was here, in New York, with her handsome husband beside her, part of this glamorous, exciting world. When Jim's hand found hers in the darkness, she squeezed it tightly, her heart so full of happiness that she felt, once again, that it might burst. It was too much, and yet, somehow, it was just enough. It was her life now. And it was just beginning.
